description: Team of two person from thailand
summary:
FireLine joins NASA’s two active-fire records into one consistent record from 2001 to today, and puts it in a free web app anyone can use.

MODIS has mapped fires since 2000 and is retiring, and VIIRS is taking over. But VIIRS sees about 2.6 times more fire in the same places because its pixels are finer and catch small fires. Joining the two raw records makes worldwide fire look up 139%, when it actually fell 10%.

Using 350 million NASA FIRMS hotspots, we built a model that converts VIIRS onto the MODIS scale. It combines a regional model, an XGBoost model that uses fire power, nearby fires, season and MODIS’s 16-day orbit, and local tuning. On years the model never saw, 96% of the world’s fire activity is within ±10% of MODIS.

The web app lets anyone pick a country, province or area and see 26 years of fire activity, compare each month with normal, view every hotspot on the map, and download the data.

This matters because fire trends guide decisions on haze, land management and fire policy. FireLine keeps NASA’s long fire record trustworthy after MODIS ends.
details:
What it does

FireLine turns NASA’s two active-fire records, MODIS (2000 onward) and VIIRS (2012 onward), into one consistent record from 2001 to today, and puts it in a free web app.

The two sensors don’t count fire the same way. VIIRS pixels are about 7 times finer, so it detects many small fires MODIS misses and records about 2.6 times more fire. Joining the raw records creates a false fire boom: worldwide fire looks up 139% when it actually fell 10%. In Northern Thailand it looks up 218% when it fell 11%.

How it works

  1. Data: 350 million NASA FIRMS hotspots, from MODIS Collection 6.1 (Terra, Aqua) and VIIRS 375 m (Suomi NPP, NOAA-20). We used the yearly archives and the daily API. We keep vegetation fires with good confidence.
  2. Common unit: both sensors are counted as “fire cell-days”, one 0.1° square (about 11 km) on one local solar day, so they can be compared directly.
  3. Regional model: a logistic regression for each world region estimates the chance that MODIS also saw each VIIRS fire.
  4. Context model: XGBoost refines that estimate using fire power, nearby fires, earlier days, place, season, and where MODIS is in its 16-day orbit cycle.
  5. Local tuning: a factor for each 1° cell and each season, pulled toward its region where data is thin. Satellite outage days are screened out.

Before 2012 the record is MODIS. After that it is VIIRS converted to the MODIS scale.

Results

We fitted the model on 2012–2018 and tested it on 2019–2021, which it never saw. 96% of the world’s fire activity is in 5° areas within ±10% of MODIS, and 90% month by month. For comparison, two identical VIIRS sensors reach 94%. Worldwide, every year from 2012 to 2024 is within 2% of MODIS.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Researchers and agencies get fire trends from 2001 that don’t jump when the sensor changes.
  • Local fire and air-quality teams can see whether this season is worse than normal for their own province.
  • Journalists, teachers and students get checked numbers for any place, with CSV downloads.
  • NASA’s 26-year fire record can continue after MODIS ends. This has already been tested by a real event: when Suomi NPP stopped on 2 November 2026, FireLine switched to NOAA-20 and the record continued.

Tools

  • Python, NumPy, pandas and PyArrow for processing.
  • scikit-learn (logistic regression) for the regional model, and XGBoost for the context model.
  • JavaScript, Leaflet and SVG for the web app, served by Python’s built-in web server.
  • Data from NASA FIRMS, an Esri basemap and Natural Earth borders.
  • Claude Code as an AI assistant for writing and checking code.
  • No special hardware: everything runs on one laptop (about 12 GB of RAM).

What makes it creative

  • We found that MODIS’s view of a place swings with its 16-day orbit cycle, and we made that a model input. It became the most important input and raised monthly agreement from 85% to 90%.
  • Instead of chasing 100%, we measured a fair ceiling by comparing two identical VIIRS sensors with each other.
  • The app turns 26 years of satellite data into a simple “burning calendar”, with years as rows and months as columns, that anyone can read.

Factors we considered

  • Fair testing: we held out whole years, scored on them, and ran a second test on 2022–2023.
  • Data quality: we flagged 272 satellite outage days automatically and found and fixed undercounted days at year boundaries in the original files.
  • Proof, not guesswork: we switched off each model input to show it helps, and dropped ideas that didn’t.
  • Honesty about limits: Western Europe reads about 19% high, agreement drops from 2022 as MODIS degrades, and small fires only VIIRS sees count for little. Raw VIIRS stays in the app.
  • Accessibility: the app needs only Python and a browser.
